Q: Why the libc++ std::vector internally keeps three pointers instead of one pointer and two sizes? A:

One of the rationale is probably due to historical reasons. Alexander Stepanov’s original SGI STL treated iterators as the fundamental abstraction, so making the most common iterator operations (begin/end) as cheap as possible would be desirable. All the containers in the C++ STL are based on iterators, therefore it's a natural decision for almost all later STL implementations to use that format. The pros are:

  • end() returns end_ directly
  • push_back() is very fast

The cons of this: size(), capacity() and empty() need 2 memory loads. The former 2 also need a subtraction and a division. This is especially bad for struct sizes that are not a power of 2. But it's likely that those are rarely called enough compared to end() to worth optimizing

Nowadays many real programs call size() / empty() far more often than they compare iterators (especially with hardening/assertions enabled). So LLVM’s libc++ has introduced a new size-based std::vector ABI which changes the internal representation from three pointers to one pointer and two integers (begin_, size_, capacity_)

tl;dr We can significantly improve the runtime performance of std::vector by changing its representation from three pointers to one pointer and two integers. This document explains the details of this change, along with the justifications for making it.

With the new layout end() has to compute begin_ + size_ every time and push_back() is less efficient, but

  • size(), empty() and capacity() need only a single memory load

  • Address calculations from size_ and capacity_ are also simple, because we need multiplication by sizeof(value_type) instead of division.

    For powers of 2 obviously it's trivial. But for values that are not powers of 2, sizeof(value_type) is usually quite small, so on most RISC architectures you can embed the value directly in the immediate field of the mul or instruction, or convert to a series of add/shift, whereas divide-by-constant will be converted into a multiplication of a very large number that needs more instructions to construct. In x86 many small multiplications can be even done with lea instruction without needing imul

    Besides, the larger the struct, the higher chance its size is not a power of 2, so the size-based vector wins in a lot of cases

  • Allow smaller object size when we don't need to support vectors spanning the whole address space. Using 32-bit size we can have a smaller vector struct that support 232 × sizeof(value_type) GB. You can simply write an allocator that uses 32-bit size directly

Their production load tests found that

  • With libc++ hardening enabled, the size-based vector is significantly faster

  • Without hardening the difference is neutral or sometimes slightly positive

    That's because even though end() is now costlier, the codegen is generally better due to the small multiplication as mentioned above

That means the size-based layout is a win regardless of hardening being enabled or not

The benchmark details are internal, but you can try the new ABI or check out boost::container::vector which also uses this layout. Fun fact: boost::container::vector also has various other optimizations, like the ability to do in-place expand, so it may be better than std::vector in many cases

See also Breaking std::vector's ABI for performance gains

Q: How to find duplicate records in codeigniter A: 
SELECT username, email, COUNT(*)
FROM users
GROUP BY username, email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

Group and find it

Q: "List columns" statements when querying Databricks via ODBC A:

MissingSchemaAction.AddWithKey makes the data adapter fetch primary key and column metadata, which triggers SQLColumns calls under the hood. Those are your "Listing columns" statements. Drop it and see if they disappear:

$adapter.MissingSchemaAction = [System.Data.MissingSchemaAction]::Add

Also, your driver is 2.11 from 2024. Version 2.9+ onwards added EnableCurlDebugLogging and better metadata caching, and how SQLColumns is served, so it might be worthwhile upgrading.

And worth setting below in the DSN:

Min_TLS=1.2
SSP_UseNativeQuery=1
Catalog=dev
Schema=foo

Q: Reusing build phase for multiple targets in Xcode A:

The way to do this is to have a script phase that references a file from your project with the script content, so that the important parts are shared.

A build phase in Xcode can only be in one target.

Q: Can't Call Action method using JavaScript,the request is not even reaching the Action method A:

The key issue was using [FromBody] with IFormFile. Since the request is sending FormData, [FromForm] is the correct binding. The fetch URL also needed to be root-relative: /Admin/Import. 👍

Glad you got it working! 🙌

Q: Err.Raise() is ignoring custom description and source A:

On Error GoTo 0 statement should be used before throwing the custom error from within the class property. Like this

Private pValue As Double

Public Property Let Value(v As Double)
    If v < 0 Then
        On Error GoTo 0
        Err.Raise vbObjectError + 1, "error source", "error description"
    Else
        pValue = v
    End If
End Property

In case of using VBA over Mac the workaround is not to propagate the error across the class boundary but to handle it within the class and return custom error to the caller.

Q: jsTree getting id of the selected node as array A:

Since data.changed.selected seems to return an array containing the id as the first element, you need to access the id using:

var id = data.changed.selected[0];

Now id will contain the actual id instead of an array.
